- ‌**gula** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Gula.

mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Gula ‌place ​healing, medicine ​at ​the ​center of ​a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

​Gula appears ‌in ​mesopotamian ‌tradition as ​healing, ​medicine. The ​name's ​meaning, ​"The great ‌one", ​shapes ‌the narratives ​told ‌about ​this figure.

### ‌Worship ​and ‌Memory (Cult)

​Devotees ​and ‌later tradition-keepers ‌preserved ‌Gula in ​ritual, ​text, ‌and iconography, ​ensuring ​the ‌name survived ​into ​the ‌modern scholarly ​record.

‌The ​myths of ​Gula ​survive ​in fragments, ‌summaries, ‌and ​later retellings. ‌Each ​version reflects ​the ‌interests ‌of its ‌tellers ‌— ​poets, priests, ‌philosophers, ​and ​scholars. The ​PuniCodex ‌entry ​does not ​privilege ​a ‌single version; ​it ​gathers the ​attestations ‌so ​that readers ‌can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Gula ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

archaeology.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Gula ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Mesopotamian ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌𒀭𒄖𒆷, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​healing ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Gula** ​(*gula*) — ‌Healing, ‌Medicine · ​The great ​one ​— belongs ​to ​the Mesopotamian ‌tradition, ​where it ​is catalogued ‌under ​the domain ‌"Healing, ​Medicine". The ‌name ​means "The ​great one"[^1].

​**Gula** ​is the ​great ‌healing goddess ​of ‌Mesopotamia — ​**'The ‌Great One,' ​Lady of ‌Isin, ​wife of ‌Ninurta, ​and divine ​patroness ‌of medicine**. ‌Doctors, exorcists, ‌and ​suffering patients ​alike ‌called on ​her ​to look ‌kindly on ​the ​sick; her ‌dogs ​stood guard ‌at ​the gates ​of her ​temples ​for over ‌a ‌thousand years.[^2]

​PuniCodex ‌records the ​canonical scholarly ​spelling ‌**Gula** and ‌serves ‌its temple ‌at ​[its temple](https://punicodex.com/gula/). ‌The displayed ​form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a description ​computed ​from the ​displayed ‌form itself. ​The plain ​ASCII ​form *gula* ‌contains ​the same ‌letters: ​no recovered ‌diacritics or ​special ‌encoding is ‌claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, capitalization, ‌provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name ‌is ‌attested ​in Cuneiform ​as ​**𒀭𒄖𒆷**. ​Etymologically ​it ‌means ​"The ​great ‌one"[^1].

The ​canonical ‌spelling ​**Gula** ‌matches ​the ​conventional ​scholarly ​romanization. The ​plain ‌ASCII ​form ‌*gula* ​contains ‌the ​same ‌letters, so ​no ‌lost ​diacritics ​or ‌encoding ‌transition ‌is ​claimed. The ​editorial ‌work ​is ​to ‌fix ​one ​reviewed ‌reference spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization ​and ​provenance, ​and ​keep ‌the ‌original evidence ​visible. ‌The ​displayed ​form ‌is ‌ASCII-equivalent ‌— ‌a description ​computed ‌from ​the ​displayed ​form ‌itself.

​The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ‌**g** ​→ ​**G** ​— ‌Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**u** → ​**u** ‌— ​Same
- ‌**l** ‌→ ​**l** ​— ​Same
- **a** ​→ ‌**a** ‌— ​Same

meditation.body: Gula ​embodies a ‌proposition ‌most ancient ​theologies only ​imply: ​that **healing ​is ​a form ‌of greatness**. ​Her ​very name ‌is ​the Akkadian ‌word for ​'great' ‌in the ​feminine ​— as ​if the ​culture ​had looked ‌for ​the largest ‌possible ​title and ‌given it ​to ‌the one ​who ‌closes wounds. ​The Babylonian ​doctor, ‌standing between ‌the ‌drug list ​and the ​incantation, ‌addressed her ​before ​both, acknowledging ‌that technique ​without ​mercy is ‌not ​medicine. There ‌is ​something striking ​in a ​warrior ​civilization's supreme ‌goddess ‌of care ​being the ‌wife ​of its ​storm-god: ‌the spear ‌and the ‌bandage ‌married. To ​read ‌her hymns ​is to ​watch ​a civilization ‌think ​through suffering ​— ​not explaining ‌it away, ​as ​Job's comforters ​tried, ‌but giving ​it a ‌face ​that looks ‌back, ​'soothes the ‌heart,' and ‌sometimes ​says yes. ​That ​is a ​theology a ‌sickbed ‌can actually ​use.[^1]
